brief.scenario: Mr Winstanley, 35, was bitten on the right forearm by his neighbour's pet dog 3 hours ago. There are two puncture wounds and a 2 cm ragged laceration that bled. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medicines. He grew up in the UK and had a tetanus booster 15 years ago.
brief.task: Discuss your assessment and management with the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Three separate decisions: the wound, antibiotics, and tetanus.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating tetanus as the whole answer, or giving immunoglobulin to every bite.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd examine for tendon, nerve and vessel injury, then irrigate thoroughly."

grid.label: Assesses the bite
grid.fail: Cleans and dresses it without checking depth or hand function.
grid.pass: Checks depth, tendon function, sensation and circulation; asks about the dog and time since the bite.
grid.high: Refers for specialist exploration if a penetrating wound involves tendon, nerve, artery, joint or bone; X-ray if a tooth fragment is suspected.

grid.label: Wound care
grid.fail: Sutures the laceration closed without irrigating it.
grid.pass: Thorough irrigation and debridement of devitalised tissue under local anaesthetic.
grid.high: Leaves the punctures open; leaves the laceration open or closes it loosely, and arranges early wound review.

grid.label: Antibiotic prophylaxis
grid.fail: Gives no antibiotics, or says every bite needs them.
grid.pass: Offers prophylaxis: the dog bite broke the skin, drew blood and includes puncture wounds. Co-amoxiclav for 3 days.
grid.high: Doxycycline plus metronidazole if penicillin-allergic. Would also consider prophylaxis for hand, foot or face bites, diabetes, immunosuppression or asplenia.

grid.label: Classifies the tetanus risk
grid.fail: Calls it a clean wound, or calls every bite high risk.
grid.pass: Tetanus-prone (animal bite with punctures) but low risk: no heavy contamination, extensive devitalised tissue or surgery delayed beyond 6 hours.
grid.high: Knows pet saliva should not carry spores unless the dog roots in soil or lives on a farm; individual risk assessment decides.

grid.label: Tetanus vaccine and immunoglobulin
grid.fail: Gives immunoglobulin for this wound, or nothing because he 'had all his jabs'.
grid.pass: Adequately primed but last dose over 10 years ago: immediate reinforcing dose of vaccine (Td/IPV); no immunoglobulin.
grid.high: For a high-risk wound would add tetanus immunoglobulin 250 IU (500 IU if over 24 hours) at a different site.

grid.label: Safety-netting and wider risks
grid.pass: Explains signs of infection and to return if they appear, worsen, or fail to improve within 24 to 48 hours of antibiotics.
grid.high: Asks where it happened: a bite abroad or from a bat needs a rabies risk assessment; considers safeguarding in children or vulnerable adults.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you manage this bite?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Clean it, put in a few stitches and a dressing.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, it's only a small bite and the dog is a pet.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: If it were, what would he need?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nothing: he had all his childhood jabs and a booster. Actually, to be safe I'd give tetanus immunoglobulin too.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you assess this bite?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd look at the depth, test tendon function, sensation and circulation in the hand, and ask about the dog and when it happened.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Thorough irrigation and debridement of any devitalised tissue under local anaesthetic.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes. It's a dog bite that has broken the skin and drawn blood, with puncture wounds, so I'd offer co-amoxiclav for 3 days.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes, an animal bite with punctures. But there's no heavy contamination, no extensive devitalised tissue and no delay to surgery, so it's low risk.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What tetanus treatment does he need?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: He's adequately primed but his last dose was over 10 years ago, so an immediate reinforcing dose of Td/IPV. No immunoglobulin.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd tell him to come back if it becomes red, swollen or discharges, or isn't improving within 24 to 48 hours on antibiotics.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you assess this bite?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Depth, tendon function, sensation and circulation. If it penetrated a tendon, nerve, artery, joint or bone, it needs specialist exploration; an X-ray if I suspected a tooth fragment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd irrigate and debride it first. The punctures stay open; the laceration I'd leave open or close loosely, because closing a contaminated bite traps bacteria. I'd arrange early review.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He says he's allergic to penicillin.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then doxycycline with metronidazole. And even for a smaller bite, I'd consider prophylaxis on the hand, foot or face, or if he were diabetic, immunosuppressed or asplenic.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why isn't this a high-risk tetanus wound?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Pet saliva shouldn't contain spores unless the dog roots in soil or lives on a farm. Here there's no heavy contamination or extensive devitalised tissue, and he'll be treated within 6 hours.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What would change your tetanus management?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A high-risk wound. He'd need the reinforcing dose plus tetanus immunoglobulin, 250 IU, or 500 IU if more than 24 hours had passed, in a different site.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Where it happened. A bite abroad or from a bat needs a rabies risk assessment with UKHSA. And if the patient were a child, I'd think about safeguarding.

failures.move: Suturing a bite laceration closed without irrigation and debridement.
failures.consequence: Traps bacteria in a contaminated wound; infection and breakdown follow.

failures.move: Withholding antibiotics from a dog bite that broke the skin with puncture wounds.
failures.consequence: Misses prophylaxis that NICE recommends offering for this wound.

failures.move: Giving tetanus immunoglobulin for a low-risk wound in a primed adult.
failures.consequence: Uses a blood product without indication; the reinforcing vaccine dose is what he needs.

failures.move: Dressing the wound without testing tendon function or sensation.
failures.consequence: A divided tendon or nerve is missed until repair is harder.

recovery.line: Separately from tetanus, I need to decide on antibiotics for the bite itself, and on how to manage the wound.
I'd irrigate and debride first, then leave it open or close it loosely, because it's a contaminated bite.

knowledge.fact: Dog bite that broke the skin and drew blood: offer prophylaxis if deep, puncture or crush, significant tissue damage, visibly contaminated, or penetrating bone, joint, tendon or vessels. Consider it for high-risk sites or comorbidities.
Co-amoxiclav first choice; doxycycline with metronidazole if penicillin-allergic. Prophylaxis 3 days, treatment 5 days.
High-risk tetanus-prone: heavy contamination with spore-containing material, extensive devitalised tissue, or surgery delayed over 6 hours.

Adequate priming is 3 or more doses. Last dose over 10 years ago: reinforcing dose, plus immunoglobulin only if high risk. Unprimed or uncertain: vaccine and immunoglobulin for any tetanus-prone wound.
UK terrestrial animals are rabies-free; bats and bites abroad need a risk assessment.

recall.think: Missed tendon injury; wound infection; tetanus.
recall.say: "Low-risk tetanus-prone: booster, no immunoglobulin, plus antibiotics."

partner.opening: This man has been bitten on the forearm by a dog. Talk me through how you would manage him.

reveals.trigger: Candidate examines the forearm and hand
reveals.finding: Two puncture wounds and a 2 cm ragged laceration on the volar mid-forearm, with a narrow rim of bruised skin edge. No visible dirt. Full finger flexion against resistance; sensation and radial pulse normal.
The neighbour's vaccinated pet, lives in a town flat. The bite happened in the neighbour's garden in the UK.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about vaccinations and allergies
reveals.finding: Full childhood vaccinations in the UK; tetanus booster at 20 after a cut. No allergies. No diabetes or immunosuppression.

push.question: Would you close the laceration?
push.expect: Irrigate and debride first; leave open or close loosely.

push.question: Does he need antibiotics?
push.expect: Yes: offer co-amoxiclav for 3 days for a dog bite that drew blood with punctures.

push.question: Is the wound tetanus-prone, and how risky?
What does he need for tetanus?
push.expect: Reinforcing dose of Td/IPV now; no immunoglobulin.

curveballs.prompt: The dog lives on a farm and the wound is packed with soil and manure.
curveballs.safeAnswer: High-risk tetanus-prone: reinforcing vaccine dose plus tetanus immunoglobulin 250 IU at a different site; thorough debridement.

curveballs.prompt: Actually, he was bitten by a street dog on holiday in Thailand two days ago.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Wash the wound thoroughly and get an urgent rabies risk assessment with UKHSA for post-exposure treatment.

curveballs.prompt: He can't bend the tip of his ring finger.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Possible flexor tendon injury: refer to the hand team for exploration and repair in theatre.
